title: Pati Patni Aur Woh Do Spent ₹60 Crore to Recover Half. Now It's Netflix's Problem.
excerpt: Ayushmann Khurrana's sequel grossed ₹53.84 crore in 12 days. The mid-budget Bollywood film is in intensive care.
body:
Here is what ₹60 crore buys you in Bollywood in 2026: Ayushmann Khurrana, Sara Ali Khan, Rakul Preet Singh, Wamiqa Gabbi, a sequel to a film people actually remember, Mudassar Aziz directing, Bhushan Kumar's T-Series and Juno Chopra's BR Studios producing, and a May 15 release date with no direct competition. All of that, and twelve days later, Pati Patni Aur Woh Do has grossed ₹53.84 crore worldwide. It has recovered barely 56 percent of its budget.

Netflix is reportedly circling for a late June premiere. The theatrical window is, for all practical purposes, over.

### The Ayushmann Paradox

Ayushmann Khurrana made his career on a specific thesis: that Indian audiences would show up for a ₹30-40 crore film with a social message if it was funny enough and self-aware enough. Vicky Donor proved it. Badhaai Ho proved it. Andhadhun proved it. Shubh Mangal Zyada Saavdhan proved it. He was the mid-budget king, and the mid-budget space was his alone.

Pati Patni Aur Woh Do is not a bad film. Reviews describe it as a "decent entertainer" — the kind of faint praise that translates directly to a ₹3 crore opening day. Khurrana plays Prajapati Pandey, a forest officer in Prayagraj navigating marriage to a journalist wife (Wamiqa Gabbi) with the expected misunderstandings, third-party complications, and climactic apology. The supporting cast — Vijay Raaz, Tigmanshu Dhulia — does its job. The songs exist.

But the ₹60 crore budget changes the equation entirely. This is not a mid-budget bet anymore. This is a big-budget comedy without big-budget names. In 2026, the only Bollywood comedies that work at this scale are franchise properties (Dhurandhar, Golmaal) or films led by the three Khans. Khurrana is respected, admired, and not a ₹60 crore star.

### Chand Mera Dil Didn't Help

The release of Chand Mera Dil on May 22 — a week into Pati Patni Aur Woh Do's run — didn't destroy its screens, but it split an already thin audience further. Two mid-tier Hindi films competing for the same urban multiplex demographic in the same month is the kind of scheduling that makes trade analysts write long threads about Bollywood's self-inflicted wounds.

Day 12 brought in just ₹1.40 crore. The India gross stands at ₹46.29 crore. Star Wars: The Mandalorian and Grogu, opening the same week, took whatever IMAX and premium screens were left.

### The OTT Safety Net

For NRIs, the math is simpler: you'll watch this on Netflix in about five weeks. It's the kind of film that plays perfectly on a laptop — light, unchallenging, familiar faces, and a runtime that doesn't demand you rearrange your evening. Ayushmann's previous films — Dream Girl 2, Article 15, Bala — all found their real audience on streaming. Pati Patni Aur Woh Do will too.

The question is whether that's enough. T-Series spent ₹60 crore on a theatrical bet. Netflix will pay a fraction of that for the digital rights. The theatrical-to-OTT pipeline works as insurance, but it doesn't work as a business model unless the theatrical number justifies the budget. This one doesn't.

### What This Means for Bollywood's Middle

The middle of Bollywood — the ₹40-80 crore film that isn't a spectacle and isn't a small indie — is in crisis. Dhurandhar 2 made ₹1,850 crore. Regional cinema is thriving. But films like Pati Patni Aur Woh Do exist in a no-man's-land: too expensive to be scrappy, too modest to be an event. The audience has decided that if a film isn't unmissable, they'll wait for OTT.

Ayushmann Khurrana will be fine. He always is. But the version of Bollywood he represented — smart, mid-range, theatrically viable — may already be gone.

Netflix will have it by July. Your couch will be the venue. The popcorn is optional.
author: Diaspora Desk
